why: It sets out, in order from front to back, the division our residences follow at a smaller scale, and it is candid that "naka-oku" is not strictly a historical term. Its limits are that it describes the palaces of castle lords, far above a provincial posting.
It gives the Chinese pairing of stage and temple as a comparison. Its limits: much of it about Hong Kong and southern China today; the setting's village default is Japanese.

It gives the room sequence of two surviving upper-samurai houses of about 1,000 to 1,200 koku, closer in scale to a provincial posting than a daimyo palace. Its limits are that it is unsigned popular writing on a company-produced site; that the Nomura house as it stands is, by the page's own account, smaller than the period house, and its audience room and raised jodan-no-ma were moved in from the house of a Kitamae-ship owner at Daishoji - a merchant's house, not a samurai's - so the order of its rooms, the butsuma beyond the audience room included, is a later assembly and not that house's own period sequence; and that the Kuchiba main house's date (late 18th to early 19th century) is hedged.

It names the several places a butsuma was set in a house, which is the choice our residence plans make. Its limits are that its placements in a house are drawn from farmhouses and the imperial palace, and its one warrior example, the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa's Tōgu-dō, is a separate chapel hall rather than a room of a residence, so nothing in it places a butsuma in a samurai house; that it gives no era for the farmhouse placements, which it describes in the present tense of surviving houses, so they may be Edo-period or later; and that the six-mat butsuma behind the oku-no-ma or zashiki is a practice of districts where the Shin sect was strong, not a general one.
It puts the first arch at the approach's start. Its limits: with no distances.

It says in so many words that the district intendant lived with the family in the residence inside the compound, which is the arrangement our postings follow. Its limits are that the residence it walks through is not the Edo building but a reconstruction finished in 1996 from an 1830 plan of the compound, so its rooms, its kitchen and its three stories are a modern rebuilding of one building's last Edo layout; who lived there is a matter of the record, not of the rebuilding. Takayama was also an unusually large office, a gundai's office from 1777 rather than an ordinary daikan's.

It dates the taking of shrine lands that stands between an Edo precinct and every Meiji-or-later register figure. Its limits: its Meiji section is two sentences resting on one forestry-encyclopedia citation (Shimada 1984). It dates the orders and says they took the shrines' granted domains, but it says nothing of the precinct itself: it does not say that the 1871 order took the land outside the precinct, or that the 1875 rules cut the precinct down to what the rites needed. Nor does it say what either took from an ordinary village shrine, which seldom held a granted domain. For those steps it carries only the dates.

It describes the family bath of noble and warrior houses around 1600 as a one-person tub with a built-on hearth in a corner of the doma, which is where a residence's bath sat and how small it was. Its limits are that the sentence is dated by the one before it to the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, so it describes the early Edo house rather than the later one; that it gives no dimensions; and that it cites no period source, while the Heibonsha Sekai Daihyakka excerpt on the same page says that until about the first half of the early modern period "furo" meant the steam bath, and that soaking in a hot-water tub became the main way of bathing only in the later Edo period, so the one-person tub is this entry's account of one form of house bath, not the only form a warrior house could have had.

It is where a travelling official of rank actually slept, and it names the three things a honjin was allowed that an inn was not: a front gate, a genkan with a shikidai and a jodan-no-ma. Its limits are that it is one the article itself flags as inadequately sourced: the sentences naming who lodged there, the front gate, the shikidai genkan and the jodan-no-ma carry no footnote, and the closer work its bibliography names, Okuma Yoshikuni's 1942 study of the Tokaido post stations and their honjin (National Diet Library Digital Collections), was not read; that a honjin was a post town's lodging house kept by a commoner family, not a samurai's residence or an office; and that it does not say where in the house the jodan-no-ma lay.

It establishes that a residence of the Edo period had amado along its openings, stowed in a tobukuro by day and shut against the night, weather and cold. Its limits are that the Britannica sentence on daytime storage describes the modern house as much as the Edo one; that the dated examples are the rulers' great buildings (Hideyoshi's Jurakudai; the Ninomaru Palace of Nijo Castle as the oldest survivor), and none says when the tobukuro-stowed amado reached a lesser samurai house - the only humbler Edo-period form it names is the townhouse shopfront's drop-in boards, stowed behind a lintel; and that none says how a household used the shutters of rooms it was not living in.

It is a signed encyclopedia article by an architectural historian that sets the warrior's stable apart from the farmer's and names what the warrior's held, which is what a posting's stable is drawn from. It gives the formal stable's length and a farm stall's size but no depth for a warrior's stall and no count of horses for any rank; its formal form is that of the sixteenth- and early seventeenth-century sources it names. That formal stable and Hikone's 21 bays are the stables of top-rank residences and of a great daimyo's castle, far larger than any posting's, so they bound a posting's stable from above and are not a model to copy. The Kinki farm stable's 3 m comes from modern studies of surviving farmhouses, with no date given, not from a record of the period.

It gives, in its own English, the warrior stable as a building of its own, its length in bays from the carpenters' manual and the Ichijodani excavation, and its stalls one bay wide on raised timber floors, the figures a posting's stable is sized from. It says none of the classic warrior stables survives, so it describes them from a manual, an excavation and a shrine's miniature; it gives a stall's width and not its depth, and it never says how long a bay is. Its classic stable is a great lord's: a shoin-style building from the Asakura daimyo's mansion, with a tatami-floored suite for retainers. The same entry records simpler warrior stables, such as the late 17th-century one at Hikone, whose stalls have timber slats laid on the earth. So raised timber floors are the top of the range, not the rule for a lesser posting's stable.

It says where a common house put its sunken hearth, in the floor of a room beside the earth-floored doma or kitchen or in the doma itself, which is what a plan's irori is checked against. Its placement passage is footnoted to a 2008 dictionary of folk implements (絵引 民具の事典) and a Chiba Prefectural Central Museum teaching page. It gives no era: its traditional house is the minka as it stood until the irori went out of use in the 1950s and 60s. It says placement varied by region: usually the center of the floored part, in some regions its edge beside the doma, and in the Nanbu magariya the doma itself. It describes the minka, the house of farmers and townspeople, not the samurai house, and it is Japanese practice only, with nothing to say about the Chinese-modeled half of the setting.

It says plainly that a samurai house's kitchen was board-floored and that, its doma being small, the kamado could stand on the board floor, which is the choice a residence's kitchen hearth is drawn from. It names no source for that sentence, and its general rule that the kamado stood on the doma is written beside a passage on commoners' rowhouses. Its samurai sentence is in its Edo-period section and is illustrated by a middle-rank retainer's house, so it speaks for the kitchens of middle and lower samurai, not for a great lord's residence, whose large kitchen (the post's own header picture is a daimyo's ōdaidokoro) is another scale of place.

It gives the width of a highway where it passed through a castle town, the kind of road a compound's front gate might open onto. The figure is rounded ("roughly"), and it is one road in one domain. The page ranks the Saigoku road as the most important side highway after the Five Highways, a main trunk route from Kyoto to Shimonoseki, so its width is a top figure for the road a compound faces, not the width of an ordinary town street. The page also does not say whether the width is the road's width inside the town or along its whole route.

It shows raising dogs for hawking as a recognized trade, and a domain lord hunting with dogs and caring for one himself. The definitions are entries that say nothing of where the dogs were kept, and their only dated example is a court text of 834 (the Ruiju Sandai Kyaku), so they show the trade in the Heian court, not in the Edo period. The Taketa story is a local place-name tradition from a 1978 town history, told as hearsay; it may be a folk explanation of an older name, and the hunt it describes is not said to be a hawking hunt.

It is the plainest readable account that the warrior elite hunted with hawks and dogs, and of who kept the dogs in the shogun's service. Its detail on staffing is the shogun's establishment, not a provincial household's, its staff counts are footnoted to a popular trivia book rather than to period records, and it describes no kennel building. It also records that the dog-handlers were under the chief falconer only until 1729, when they were given their own head under the gunnery commander as hunting turned to the gun, so it carries that arrangement for the earlier Edo period only.

It attests boar hunting with packs of native dogs in the Kii mountains, the kind of hunt a lord who hunts boar would keep dogs for. Its account of traditional hunting describes hunters with guns and is undated, and the figure of three or four dogs to a hunter carries no citation in the article, so it gives the shape of the hunt and only a rough count; the story of a castle lord's hunt is a legend.
unsettled: The evidence is an undated account of hunters with guns, which the period table cannot place before or after 1868.

why: It says in so many words that a study could be a room or a building, which is the question a detached study raises. Its historical examples are upper-class houses of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods (from the Azuma Kagami, which does not say whose house), medieval temples, and the early modern imperial and retired emperor's palaces, and it names no Edo-period warrior house. It gives no size for a detached study. Its only room sizes, six and seven mats, are Natsume Soseki's Meiji-era study, a modern house, and not a premodern figure; the "two to four ken" it gives is the width of a bookshelf in the court's gakumonsho, not of a room.

It defines the household's own entrance, kept apart from the formal one for the family's daily comings and goings. They give no plan, no position (the entrance is set up in addition to the front one, not placed beside it, and "back entrance" is given as a synonym), no rank, and nothing about the kitchen door. That the family used it instead of the kitchen's door is our reading, not the dictionary's. Its earliest example, under the reading naigenkan, is a joruri of 1714: the word's first recorded use, not the date of any building. The reading uchigenkan is first cited from a 1930 novel. It says nothing of a Chinese house.

It attests the other historical form of regular dealing across a land border: a post on each side of the line, a few hundred feet apart, with officials of both handling diplomacy and disputes. Wikipedia tags it as lacking inline citations and needing factual verification, it says it is a summary of Clifford M. Foust's monograph <cite>Muscovite and Mandarin</cite> (1969), and its passage on the two posts a few hundred feet apart, with officials on both sides, carries no citation, so that distance is the article's and not a checked figure (Foust is the closer source); the parties are the Russian and Qing empires in the eighteenth century, not domains or clans, and it describes no building where the two met.

unsettled: The page gives a modern plasterer's standard leaf size without saying what period the standard comes from.

why: It gives the reasons a granary's floor was raised, rats and damp, and where in Japan the form lasted, which is what a granary drawn on posts is checked against. Its Japanese cases are prehistoric sites and the islands and far north where the form survived; it says nothing of the earth-walled storehouses of the Edo mainland, and almost nothing of Chinese or Korean granaries, so for the Chinese side of the setting it gives the reason for the raised floor and not whether one was built.

It states what such a post was for and where it stood, which is the question a river watch on the map raises. It is a stub of two sentences, flagged since 2019 as giving no sources, speaks of coastal domains and names only posts at the mouths of two bays in Nagasaki; it gives no size, staffing or plan.

It says the guardian is kept aboard and only sometimes given a shrine on land, which bears on whether a landing had a boatmen's shrine. The passages we use (the objects kept aboard, the shrine sometimes set up on land, the fishermen and shipwrights who chiefly keep it) cite no source of their own; its references are a Japanese dictionary, a 1989 Izumo Taishakyo training manual, a shrine's website and the Shoku Nihongi. It dates a funadama festival to 758 and the name to 763 from the Shoku Nihongi, but gives no date for the customs we use, and it mixes old practice with recent (talismans placed in a boat's engine room). It speaks of seafarers and says nothing of river boatmen in particular, and its examples of land shrines (at Sumiyoshi Taisha in Osaka and in Hakodate) are not shrines at a landing.

It says what a bale is and that charcoal went in them, the objects the map draws on its barges and in its charcoal yards. It gives no dimensions, only capacities of four or six to depending on the product. Its square charcoal bales are from Hokkaido's Iburi district, and its only source for them is a 2014 oral history of the Showa era (1926-1989). They are a twentieth-century practice, not evidence that premodern charcoal was packed square.

It is the source for the bale's want of a standard size before the Meiji period, with the shogunate's and Kaga domain's figures, and for charcoal packed at weights set by grade. Its Edo-period figures (a bale of 2 to 5 to, the shogunate's 3 to 5 sho, Kaga's 5 to, and no standard size) carry no footnote of their own and rest on the article alone. Its charcoal figures are for the Iburi district of Hokkaido, taken from a 2014 collection of Showa-era oral histories of Hobetsu. They are twentieth-century practice on land settled only from the Meiji period, so they stand in for the fact that premodern charcoal was packed by grade, not for its premodern weights. It gives capacities and weights, not dimensions.

It quotes a 1794 manual of rural administration on where a village storehouse was built and says where tax rice went from it, which places a granary in its chain and on its ground. They say nothing of how the storehouse was built, the Nihon Kokugo Daijiten says not every village had one (several villages might share one, or the headman's own storehouse was used instead), so a storehouse in every village is not theirs to give, and they date the shogunate's order for village-built storehouses to 1789 where other pages give 1790.

unsettled: The bale is dated only to the mid-Showa period, which may fall on either side of the 1955 cut-off for Japan.

why: It establishes the steelyard as China's traditional weighing tool and describes its working. It is a brief article, flagged since 2014 as listing no sources, dates nothing: it gives no origin or history for the steelyard and no scale for heavy ones, so its use in imperial China rests only on its word "traditional" (传统) and its note that steelyard-making was listed as Shanghai intangible heritage in 2019, not on any period evidence.

It says what the balance and the steelyard were each used for in Japan - the balance for valuables, the steelyard for food and daily goods - from which we infer what a weighing floor for charcoal used; the page never names charcoal, and gives no period for the two uses within Japan. Its account of the balance's weight is set in the ancient world, and its account of the two tools' uses is hedged ("it seems"). Updated 2024.

It names the construction as one of Japanese architecture's fire-resistant forms and dates Edo's spread of it for fire prevention to after the Kyoho era (1716-36). Its entries are short dictionary and encyclopedia summaries, good for the construction's form and dates rather than for measurements. They differ on the policy: Heibonsha says the spread was forced, Yamakawa says it was encouraged, and the older Heibonsha says a 1720 edict permitted it. Mypedia instead puts the edicts after the Meireki fire (1657). The 1720 edict quoted in the Nihon Kokugo Daijiten is the firmest date. Its entries concern the construction and Edo's building policy; they say nothing of what a storehouse held or of spacing between buildings.

Its entries are short Japanese dictionary and encyclopedia articles - only two of them signed (Matsuzaki Kin'ichi, Kumai Tamotsu) - one of them quoting an 1815 report by the headman of Shiba Kurumamachi in Edo, and they give the cart's size and its spread through the towns. They disagree with each other on where it spread - the 1815 report says Kyoto, Osaka and the castle towns of other provinces, while three other entries say Osaka (one says Kyoto and Osaka) used a different cart, the beka-guruma, and two say the daihachiguruma was mainly a cart of Edo and the Kanto castle towns. The bed of 8 by 2.5 shaku (about 8 by 2.5 ft) comes from one unsigned passage of an older encyclopedia edition; another entry says beds ran from 6 to 10 shaku long, the 8-shaku one being the size that named the cart. They say nothing of carts on the highways or of the width of the lanes a cart used.

It defines the practice, cites its use in a shrine record of 804, and names the two-bay, two-door hall built for it, so it is sound for what the form was and what it was called. It gives no count of how common each form was, no dates for the two-door hall, and nothing about a shrine in an office. On a shrine inside a residence it has only one passing usage: a 1771 comic tale's "aidono of the toshidana", the New Year god-shelf set up indoors, which shows the word was used for a household shelf but does not describe one. Its note that the lesser kami rank below the main one says this holds "in many cases", not always.

It states plainly that a shrine ordinarily enshrines several kami, one of them the main one, which is the practice this record needs. It is a stub that Japanese Wikipedia has flagged as short of sources since 2011, and it gives no figures for how many shrines kept more than one kami. By its own account the formal division into a main kami and secondary kami began at the Meiji-era government shrines (only the idea is older, under names such as 相殿神). It says the Meiji shrine mergers left many shrines with more secondary kami. It also says that naming a shrine's kami after the kami of the myths reached village and unranked shrines only in the Meiji era. So for a pre-Meiji village shrine it supports only that several kami could share one hall with one of them foremost, not how common that was or what those kami were called.

It is an overview of mixed footing, some passages footnoted to books on the torii and others tagged as needing a citation. It names the gates of one approach first, second and onward from the outermost, and lists a subsidiary shrine within a larger precinct (Tomouji-sha within Kitano Tenmangu) that has its own stone torii. The sentence on counting the gates carries no footnote and no date and states the convention as present usage, so it shows the naming but not that the naming is premodern. The subsidiary shrine is named only in a list of Kyoto's three curious torii, a section the article flags as possibly original research, with no source and no description: an oddity listed, not an ordinary case described. Its examples are famous shrines rather than ordinary ones, and it gives no distance from any torii to the hall it serves.

It names the guardroom at a gate as an institution of Edo castle and points to a surviving pair beside the Akamon, which supports a gatehouse set beside a gate. Its Akamon sentence rests on one footnote to the University of Tokyo's own page. It gives no sizes; the national designation record (文化遺産オンライン, 旧加賀屋敷御守殿門) is the closer source and gives each guardroom as 3 by 2 ken, single-story, with cusped gables front and back. Its gate examples are the shogun's castle and the Kaga Maeda mansion gate of 1827, built for a shogun's daughter's marriage, far above a county post; its one rural example, the Nuruyu domain border post, is nearer that scale.

It says that intendants' offices and barriers had courts too, which is what carries the court from the capital's magistracy to a county office, and it puts commoners on mats. It says only that those offices had a court, not how large it was or how it was laid out; the mats and the board veranda it describes are those of the Edo town magistracy, a capital's office, so using them at a county office is a change of scale. Its limits are that it describes the court as a garden facing the hall without saying whether it was roofed, and that it seats an accused samurai or monk on the board veranda where two other sources put samurai on the upper, tatami one.

It gives the reasons for the one surviving intendant's court's form - river cobbles for want of white sand, and a roof because of the snow - which is what lets a map choose the court's surface by its place. Its limits are that its reasons are the guide's account rather than a cited record, and that the roof over the accused is stated in the interviewer's question, the guide saying the court was made inside the building.

It is the managing body's own account of the one intendant's office whose main buildings survive, and it says the jin'ya had a court for villages' petitions as well as one for criminal cases, and that its jail stood in the town. Its limits are that it is hedged on the torture ("thought to", "reportedly"), and that Takayama was a gundai's office, larger than an ordinary intendant's.
